title: What is Structured Concurrency / `StructuredTaskScope` (ShutdownOnFailure vs ShutdownOnSuccess), and how does it eliminate orphaned tasks and simplify cancellation?
shortTitle: What is Structured Concurrency / StructuredTaskScope, and how does it eliminate orphaned tasks and simplify cancellation?

s1_definition.profdef: Structured concurrency treats a group of concurrent subtasks as a single unit of work with a bounded lifetime: if a task splits into concurrent subtasks, they must all complete before the task returns, which is enforced by `StructuredTaskScope`. You open a scope, `fork` subtasks that run on virtual threads, call `join` to wait for them, then read results, all within a try-with-resources block so the scope's `close` guarantees every subtask has finished. Two common policies are shutdown-on-failure, which cancels the remaining subtasks as soon as one fails so you can fail fast, and shutdown-on-success, which cancels the rest as soon as one succeeds so you can race for the first good result. This structure makes orphaned tasks impossible and makes cancellation automatic and reliable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a loan officer at National Bank of India who, to approve a loan, must get three checks done at once: a credit-bureau score, an income verification, and a fraud check. Structured concurrency is a strict rule that says the officer cannot leave the desk until all three helpers have returned, and if any one of them reports a hard failure, the officer immediately calls off the other two instead of wasting their time. If instead the officer only needs the fastest of several equivalent data providers to answer, the moment one answers, the others are told to stop. Nobody is left working on a request that has already been decided, and nobody is forgotten.
s1_definition.oneliner: StructuredTaskScope binds concurrent subtasks to a parent scope so they all finish before the parent returns, with shutdown-on-failure for fail-fast and shutdown-on-success for racing, eliminating orphaned tasks and making cancellation automatic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structured concurrency treats a group of concurrent subtasks as a single unit of work with a bounded lifetime: if a task splits into concurrent subtasks, they must all complete before the task returns, which is enforced by `StructuredTaskScope`. You open a scope, `fork` subtasks that run on virtual threads, call `join` to wait for them, then read results, all within a try-with-resources block so the scope's `close` guarantees every subtask has finished. Two common policies are shutdown-on-failure, which cancels the remaining subtasks as soon as one fails so you can fail fast, and shutdown-on-success, which cancels the rest as soon as one succeeds so you can race for the first good result. This structure makes orphaned tasks impossible and makes cancellation automatic and reliable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a loan officer at National Bank of India who, to approve a loan, must get three checks done at once: a credit-bureau score, an income verification, and a fraud check. Structured concurrency is a strict rule that says the officer cannot leave the desk until all three helpers have returned, and if any one of them reports a hard failure, the officer immediately calls off the other two instead of wasting their time. If instead the officer only needs the fastest of several equivalent data providers to answer, the moment one answers, the others are told to stop. Nobody is left working on a request that has already been decided, and nobody is forgotten.

**One line to remember:** StructuredTaskScope binds concurrent subtasks to a parent scope so they all finish before the parent returns, with shutdown-on-failure for fail-fast and shutdown-on-success for racing, eliminating orphaned tasks and making cancellation automatic.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem structured concurrency fixes is that unstructured concurrency, like submitting tasks to an executor and holding futures, has no enforced relationship between the parent operation and its subtasks. If the parent returns early or throws, the subtasks can keep running as orphans, consuming resources and logging confusing errors, and cancellation is manual and easy to get wrong because you have to remember to cancel every future on every error path. Error handling is scattered and leaks are common.

StructuredTaskScope enforces a parent-child structure. You open it in a try-with-resources, fork each subtask, which returns a handle and runs the work on a fresh virtual thread, then call join to wait for all subtasks to finish or for the policy to trigger shutdown, and only then do you read each subtask's result. Because the scope is closed at the end of the try block, its close method guarantees that by the time the parent operation returns, every forked subtask has either completed or been cancelled; there is simply no way to leave a subtask running past the scope. That single guarantee is what eliminates orphans.

The policy determines how the group reacts. With a shutdown-on-failure policy, the first subtask that throws triggers an interrupt of all the other still-running subtasks, so you fail fast; after join you call a throw-if-failed method that rethrows the first exception, and otherwise you collect all the results. This is the pattern for a transfer that needs several independent checks to all pass. With a shutdown-on-success policy, the first subtask that succeeds triggers cancellation of the rest, and you read the single winning result; this is the pattern for racing several equivalent sources and taking the fastest. Cancellation is cooperative through interruption, and because everything runs on virtual threads a blocked subtask that is interrupted unwinds promptly. For example you fork a credit check, an income check, and a fraud check, join, throw if any failed, and then combine the three results into a decision, and if the fraud check fails the other two are cancelled automatically. A senior nuance: structured concurrency composes with deadlines, because you can join with a timeout so the whole group is bounded in time, and it composes with scoped values, which child tasks inherit cheaply, giving you context propagation for free; the newest API iterations fold the policy into how you open the scope and provide a joiner abstraction, but the core principles, forking into a bounded scope, joining, and guaranteed shutdown, are stable, and the payoff is that concurrency now reads like ordinary structured code with clear error handling instead of a tangle of futures.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India approves a transfer only after three independent checks, a credit-bureau check, an income verification, and a fraud check, which should run concurrently for speed. With raw futures, if one check fails the others keep running as orphans and the error handling is messy. This is exactly what StructuredTaskScope with shutdown-on-failure solves — the first failure cancels the rest and the parent cannot return until all are done.

Problem 2 — For a currency rate the bank queries several equivalent providers and only needs the fastest good answer. This is exactly what shutdown-on-success solves — the first provider to answer wins and the slower ones are cancelled automatically.

The demo runs the three approval checks concurrently with a fail-fast scope and races rate providers with a first-success scope, showing that on any failure or first success the remaining subtasks are cancelled and nothing is orphaned. Classes and steps: `ApprovalChecks` (the check tasks), `TransferApprovalService` (both scopes), and `StructuredConcurrencyDemo`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an approval for Rajesh (SAV2001) needing three concurrent checks, and a currency rate raced across two providers.

Step 1 — approve opens a shutdown-on-failure scope and forks the credit, income, and fraud checks, each running on its own virtual thread concurrently, so the total time is bounded by the slowest check rather than their sum.

Step 2 — The fraud check throws after forty milliseconds. The shutdown-on-failure policy immediately interrupts the still-running credit and income checks, so they are cancelled rather than left running, and join returns.

Step 3 — throwIfFailed rethrows the fraud failure, so the method exits through the catch in the demo, and because the whole body was inside the try-with-resources, the scope's close has already guaranteed that credit and income finished unwinding; there are no orphaned subtasks continuing in the background.

Step 4 — fastestRate opens a shutdown-on-success scope and forks the fast and slow rate providers. The fast provider answers in thirty milliseconds, so the policy cancels the slow one and join returns, and result gives the winning fast rate. Both scenarios show the parent never returns until every subtask has completed or been cancelled.

```
2026-10-26 16:30:01 [WARNING] approval failed fast: FRAUD flagged SAV2001 (siblings cancelled, nothing orphaned)
2026-10-26 16:30:01 [INFO] winning RATE:1USD=83.10 (fast) (slow provider cancelled)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  FAIL-FAST (ShutdownOnFailure) — all must pass
    approve("SAV2001")  try(scope) {
      fork creditCheck ─► vthread (80ms)  ─┐
      fork incomeCheck ─► vthread (60ms)  ─┤ run concurrently
      fork fraudCheck  ─► vthread (40ms, THROWS) ─┘
        │ first failure → scope interrupts credit + income (CANCELLED)
      join() ; throwIfFailed() → rethrow FRAUD
    } close() → guarantees credit/income finished → NO ORPHANS

  RACE (ShutdownOnSuccess) — first winner
    fastestRate()  try(scope) {
      fork rateFast ─► vthread (30ms) ✓ first success
      fork rateSlow ─► vthread (200ms) → CANCELLED on first success
      join() ; result() → "1USD=83.10 (fast)"
    }

  Parent NEVER returns while a subtask still runs (bounded lifetime).
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — StructuredTaskScope Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Scope-bound fork/join: subtasks tied to a parent lifetime      │
  │    WHY: no orphans — close() waits for all forks               │
  │ Policy (Strategy): ShutdownOnFailure vs ShutdownOnSuccess      │
  │    WHY: fail-fast group vs first-winner race                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: service orchestrates; each check task does one check        │
  │ O: add a 4th check = one more fork, policy unchanged           │
  │ D: service depends on Callable tasks + scope, not threads      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Policies (as prose) ───────────────────────────────────────
  ShutdownOnFailure : first failure cancels siblings → throwIfFailed → fail fast
  ShutdownOnSuccess : first success cancels siblings → result() → race winner
  join(deadline)    : bound the whole group in time
  close()           : guarantees all subtasks done/cancelled (no orphans)

  ── State: Scope Lifecycle ────────────────────────────────────
  [OPEN] ──fork×N──→ [RUNNING] ──join──→ [JOINED] ──read results──→ [CLOSED]
             │ policy trigger (fail/success)        │
             └──────── cancel remaining ────────────┘  (all threads unwound)

  ── Call Chain (fail-fast) ────────────────────────────────────
  1. try (scope = ShutdownOnFailure)
  2.   fork credit/income/fraud  (3 virtual threads)
  3.   fraud throws → scope interrupts credit + income
  4.   join() → throwIfFailed() → rethrow
  5.   close() → all subtasks finished → no orphans
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Structured concurrency treats a group of concurrent subtasks as a single unit of work with a bounded lifetime, enforcing that if a task splits into concurrent subtasks, they must all complete before the task returns. StructuredTaskScope implements this: I open a scope in a try-with-resources, fork each subtask so it runs on its own virtual thread, call join to wait, and then read the results, and because the scope is closed at the end of the try block, its close guarantees that by the time my operation returns every subtask has either completed or been cancelled. That single guarantee is what makes orphaned tasks impossible.

This fixes the real problem with unstructured concurrency, which is that when you submit tasks to an executor and hold futures, there is no enforced relationship between the parent and its subtasks. If the parent returns early or throws, the subtasks keep running as orphans, wasting resources and logging confusing errors, and cancellation is manual, because you have to remember to cancel every future on every error path, which is easy to get wrong.

The policy decides how the group reacts. Shutdown-on-failure means the first subtask that fails triggers cancellation of all the others so I fail fast, and after join I call throw-if-failed to rethrow the first exception, otherwise I collect all results; that is the pattern when several independent checks must all pass. Shutdown-on-success means the first subtask that succeeds cancels the rest and I read the single winning result; that is the pattern for racing several equivalent sources and taking the fastest. In both cases cancellation is cooperative through interruption, and because everything runs on virtual threads, an interrupted blocked subtask unwinds promptly.

In my banking work at National Bank of India transfer approval needed a credit-bureau check, an income verification, and a fraud check to all pass, and I ran them concurrently in a shutdown-on-failure scope, so when the fraud check failed the other two were cancelled automatically and nothing was left running in the background. For currency rates I raced several equivalent providers in a shutdown-on-success scope and took the fastest answer while the slower ones were cancelled. The senior points I always add are that structured concurrency composes with deadlines, because I can join with a timeout to bound the whole group in time, and with scoped values, which child tasks inherit cheaply so context propagates for free, and that the biggest practical win is that concurrent code now reads like ordinary structured code with clear error handling, instead of a tangle of futures with manual cancellation and orphan risk.
